fullText:
Former Vice President Mike Pence and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on Sunday stressed the importance of Ukraine having the capabilities to deter Russian ballistic missile strikes.

During an interview on NewsNation's "The Hill Sunday," Pence said Russian forces have "shifted" to using high-arc ballistic missiles and cruise missiles to strike Ukraine.

Those weapons require Patriot interceptors or terminal high-altitude area defense (THAAD) interceptors, the former vice president noted. Pence on Sunday addressed the National Prayer Breakfast in Ukraine and spoke with Zelensky.

"And President Zelensky again reiterated to me what he said publicly, that he's anxious to see the United States make up to 5 percent of our Patriot resources available to make it possible for Ukraine to beat back those ballistic missile attacks," Pence told host Chris Stirewalt.

"Stopping those ballistic missile attacks essentially will in many ways take the last fighting tool out of Vladimir Putin's hands," he said, referring to the Russian president.

While President Trump granted Ukraine a license to co-produce Patriot missiles in July, analysts have emphasized it will take years before the eastern European country is able to produce a suitable amount of those weapons.

Also complicating matters is the fact that the U.S. has exhausted nearly 80 percent of its THAAD interceptors and roughly half of its Patriots during the Iran war, CNN reported earlier this month.

Pence, though, denied Sunday that the Pentagon depleting its interceptor stockpiles is hurting Ukraine.

"I don't see it that way, and I don't think … the Ukrainians do either," Pence told host Dana Bash on CNN's "State of the Union."

July marked the deadliest month for civilians in Ukraine since May 2022, according to the United Nations Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine.

Zelensky said Sunday he briefed Sens. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) and James Lankford (R-Okla.) in Kyiv on Russia's "ongoing ballistic missile terror."

The Ukrainian leader wrote on social media: "It is very important for Ukraine to have the capabilities to counter this, and implementing the decision to grant licenses for the production of Patriots could significantly help."

Pence echoed Zelensky's rhetoric, saying it is "essential" for the Trump administration and other foreign allies to continue backing Ukraine militarily.

Without further assistance, an "unprotected" Ukraine will be at risk of Russian attacks on energy infrastructure sites as the winter approaches, the former vice president stated.

"President Zelensky made it clear to me that Putin is going to use those ballistic missiles to strike, particularly not just like he did at a children's hospital this week and not just as he did it at … a shopping mall this week," Pence told Stirewalt. "But he'll use that to take out the energy infrastructure here as winter approaches."

title: Using international football to reignite Premier League dreams
description: Before his potential Premier League debut for Fulham, BBC Sport looks at the role international football has played in the development of players like Shea Charles.
fullText:
On an August afternoon at Queen Ethelburga's College in York eight years ago, Michael O'Neill could never have known he was about to set eyes upon two players who would go on to become two of his most important Northern Ireland internationals.

It was then that Shea Charles, who has just become NI's most expensive-ever player at the age of 22, and Isaac Price both donned a Northern Ireland shirt for the first time against Leeds United's Under-16s in a friendly.

The duo played as part of a Club NI side - the academy for Northern Ireland at the time - alongside the likes of Liverpool's Conor Bradley and Portsmouth's Terry Devlin.

It was the first step along an international pathway that would see the pair win senior caps as teenagers under O'Neill before they had established themselves at their clubs. Both are now among the first names on the manager's teamsheet.

In the summer window, Charles became the most expensive Northern Ireland footballer when he joined Premier League side Fulham for £30m from Southampton, who he had joined after leaving Manchester City in 2023.

"You could see straight away there was a player there," said O'Neill as he recalled the first time he watched Charles in 2018.

"I suppose that's one of the biggest pleasures we've had with this team because we've known these boys from such a young age."

Charles' rise to NI's most expensive footballer

Dallas backs Charles to thrive at Fulham

As the examples of Charles and his younger brother, Pierce, show, eligibility is key for a nation with a playing pool as small as Northern Ireland.

Sometimes players are scouted, sometimes the parents or agents of players approach the Irish FA, or clubs can alert the association to eligible players.

Sometimes, however, it is a case of being in the right place at the right time.

Joe Shields, who was head of youth recruitment at Manchester City at the time, got to know the Charles family and knew the brothers would be eligible through their mother, Mary, who comes from Northern Ireland.

After watching Shea progress, Shields contacted Andy Cousins, who was also working at City with emerging talent and with the Irish FA, and recommended that it would be good for his development to get involved in the pathway with Northern Ireland.

From there, Cousins introduced O'Neill to the Charles and Price families ahead of their debuts for the Club NI side.

While O'Neill says he was "being polite and saying hello", it also served a bigger purpose. For an up and coming player like Charles, it left a lasting impression.

"It was really cool for us, to be able to see that the senior manager had that interest in the youth team," said midfielder Charles, who has won 35 caps since making his NI debut in March 2023.

"It was really good to see that he does look at those younger age groups and for boys who maybe have a chance to come through.

"It really helped me get to know the boys, the coaches, the whole set-up and eventually going on my first senior camp and making my debut. It was really special and shows that the pathway was really important."

O'Neill says it is important for him to see the next generation of talent long before they get on the fringes of the senior team, and that the work of Andy Waterworth, director of elite player development, and his staff gives him an opportunity to be in the thick of things.

"I think we're really good at that as a small association," he said.

"With the time frame at that age, it can go quite quickly so there's lads I'm seeing in our academy and I may well be the manager that gives that player his debut."

Cousins, who said Charles "didn't have a worry in the world" at City and "just loved playing football", believes that O'Neill's work with the players at a young age allows him to trust them at senior level, which may not happen at other associations.

"It's allowed him to believe in them and put them on the pitch young and early," said Cousins, who now works as head of scouting at Chelsea alongside Shields, who is co-sporting director at Stamford Bridge.

"I think he worries less about the physical elements, and if he thinks they're going to be a really good player long term, it's about getting them in quickly to try and be at that level."

O'Neill says there are two threads to developing Northern Ireland's playing pool, through domestic-based players and those recruited through eligibility.

There are the success stories of Charles and Price, who came through at Everton before establishing himself at senior level with Standard Liege and West Brom.

But O'Neill adds that if a club releases a player or if their future is uncertain, that the JD Academy - the successor to Club NI - offers stability to help them continue to develop as footballers.

O'Neill pointed to the stories of Dan Ballard and Pierce Charles, who were released by Arsenal and Manchester City respectively, but were still selected by Northern Ireland's youth teams to continue their development.

Now, Ballard is a key player for Sunderland - alongside fellow NI defender Trai Hume - and this summer Charles re-joined Manchester City from Sheffield Wednesday before going on loan to Queen's Park Rangers.

"Their futures were very much in the balance. Pierce was released from Man City at 16, but we don't release him from Northern Ireland.

"It's very important to keep the boys involved as much as we can and try and help and support them when those difficult situations arise."

Shea Charles said the story of his brother was "really important" and it was positive for his development to stay involved with Northern Ireland.

"When Pierce left City, he always had those [Northern Ireland underage] games to play in.

"He always had a spot in those teams and was still able to show what he can do at that high level. I feel that can be the same for so many lads."

O'Neill highlighted the example of Ethan Galbraith, who won his first cap as an 18-year-old in 2019 when he was at Manchester United but only broke into the NI team with more regularity when he was 23 and working his way back up the football ladder with Leyton Orient.

With that time and patience, he is now an integral part of O'Neill's squad and earned a move to Stoke City from Swansea in the summer window.

"You can see the potential in all the young players, but their careers never go in an upward straight line all the time," O'Neill added.

"We never write young players off. We understand that at times they may have difficult times at their clubs, but that's natural. It's a competitive environment."

Despite having smaller resource compared to larger nations, O'Neill believes the IFA's scouting team "doesn't miss very much" when it comes to eligibility.

"We're constantly working at it and we're having conversations with various lads who are at different stages of their careers as well.

"I wouldn't ask a young player to do an international transfer unless I thought they genuinely had a chance to come and be a senior international. I think that's very important."

The second strand is with domestic-based players within Northern Ireland.

Of O'Neill's current squad, players like Trai Hume, Conor Bradley, Ethan Galbraith and Ruairi McConville are all graduates from the pathway.

With the next generation, Ceadach O'Neill and Braiden Graham are examples of getting senior Northern Ireland experience while still featuring at underage level for Arsenal and Everton respectively.

Both players have been in the JD Academy and featured for Irish Premiership side Linfield before they made the move to England.

Charles says that while it is a different pathway than the English club system, the benefit of training and playing together has been beneficial for his team-mates.

"The boys talk about how it was really good for them," he said.

"I'm sure it was a bit different to England, but the end goal was always the same to get to the senior squad, so credit to them."

He adds the fact that, no matter where their football journey started, that they have all come through the underage ranks together has been beneficial at senior level.

"I feel like you can see it on the pitch, with the way we play, and how we talk to each other and congratulate each other.

"When we get a bad result, you can see the way we get around each other. It's a really great group."

Before Club NI was formed, there was a community programme but the full JD Academy, as it is now known, allows the most promising young footballers in Northern Ireland to participate in a residential programme at Campbell College, as well as the benefits that come with playing international football at a young age such as nutrition and strength and conditioning.

For O'Neill, it has been one of the "biggest pluses" since he took over as manager for the first time in 2012, saying the academy has done a "phenomenal job".

"I think we have something which a lot of associations are quite jealous of," he said.

"If you're in a big country, the clubs develop the players because they've got the resources to do it, but our clubs can't do that.

"Not every player in the academy is going to go and be a professional player or will play for Northern Ireland at senior international level, but it is giving them a really good opportunity at a critical time in their development path."

While the Championship is a strong league with consistently challenging opposition, playing international football has allowed Charles to play - and hold his own - against some of the best players of the world.

In the past three years, he has faced Rodri for Spain just before they won the European Championships, Germany's Florain Wirtz, Sandro Tonali for Italy and France's midfield pairing of Aurelien Tchouameni and Adrien Rabiot.

On each occasion Charles held his own - particularly against Italy, where he was arguably the best player on the pitch against Tonali and Nicolo Barella.

On Monday night, the 22-year-old could make his Fulham debut against Xabi Alonso's Chelsea, a potential second Premier League appearance coming three years after his debut under Pep Guardiola at City.

It could be a full circle moment for Charles, as he will be reunited with Cousins and Shields, who played a role in the development of the likes of current Chelsea midfielders Cole Palmer, Morgan Rogers and Romeo Lavia, who came through at City alongside Fulham's new recruit.

"It's much easier to benchmark players when you can say that you've played against players from the Premier League or certainly the top five leagues in Europe," said Cousins.

"Especially where the Premier League is so demanding physically, to see people performing well at that level, it's much easier to trust that and to be able to sign a player.

"I think Shea will be absolutely no problem at all, as he's shown in his performances against those big teams he has played against in the last two years."

Charles agrees and says facing the world's best players has helped him prepare for the Premier League.

"To be in that Premier League environment and hopefully to make my Fulham debut on Monday would just be incredible," Charles said.

"It'll be really cool playing the best players in the world every week.

"I look forward to playing with Northern Ireland and being able to experience those games, even if it's a friendly like the Spain or France games.

"It's does prepare you for what the best players are like, so I'm really looking forward to it."

title: Wales pushing the pain barrier in bid to improve
description: BBC Sport spends a day in Wales' pre-season camp, watching players put through their paces ahead of the new WXV Global Series.
fullText:
Sweat is pouring off Alisha Joyce and Georgia Evans as they emerge exhausted from the spin bike chamber at Wales' training base.

They collapse to the floor fighting for breath as head coach Sean Lynn gives them an encouraging tap on the back.

Next door in the gym Maisie Davies changes the playlist to "It's my birthday" while the forwards go about completing their sets in search of personal bests.

And out on the artificial pitch, Ashley Beck is putting the backs through their paces, with uncapped Amy Williams catching the eye.

This is just a glimpse of life in Wales' camp and for the players three weeks of pre-season pain is almost over.

But for Lynn and the other coaches the hard work continues as they must whittle down the squad for next month's WXV Global Series.

Neumann back in Wales' extended WXV training squad

New-look Wales end losing streak with Barbarians win

Wales kick-off their campaign against South Africa at Cardiff Arms Park on 18 September before hosting USA on 26 September. They will then head out to Japan for two further Tests on 23 and 31 October.

All three opponents are ranked above 12th-placed Wales, who have lost their last nine competitive fixtures.

And despite a welcome victory over Barbarians in June, Lynn's side know they are still lacking in a number of areas, notably fitness.

It is a key focus for strength and conditioning coach Gareth Harris who is out on the main pitch encouraging the players through an intense set of interval runs.

Keira Bevan is rigged with a social media microphone as she races her opposite number to a marked cone.

"We need to work harder," Harris said.

"We know where we are from a physical perspective and it is about moving that dial forward. A lot of the girls are pretty sore, but that's okay, it's all in the plan."

The 46-strong extended squad has been in camp since 3 August and trained through soaring temperatures, but Harris - who linked up with Wales before last summer's Rugby World Cup - says the attitude has been "exceptional".

"You really see the girls going 'this is important for us'," Harris said.

"We want to be better. We want to be the best team we can be. We don't just want to turn up to the international stage, we want to dominate games.

"There's ownership of the work that they're doing and ownership of our standards and how we elevate those standards and accountability to each person.

"Everybody is going 'this is what I expect of you', which is perfect for us.

"I think we'll see a different Wales this time round."

Harris' optimism is echoed by forwards coach Steve Salvin who has come up to the vantage point of the barn balcony.

He clearly feels at home here having joined Lynn's backroom staff on a permanent basis with Ashley Beck in the summer.

"The four of us [coaches] were thrown together a little bit for the Six Nations, firefighting would be the wrong way to put it but obviously we were working in silos to get things sorted. Now we can be much more cohesive and collective around the way we go about doing things," Salvin said.

"We feel like there's growth in our set piece, our attack, our defence, we're essentially trying to cover all bases.

"During the Six Nations we performed reasonably well for probably 50 to 60 minutes, so one of the things we really need to go after for this series of games is performing for 80 minutes.

"If we do that, we'll give ourselves a much better chance of coming out the right side of the results."

Wales have only tasted success twice since Lynn took over in March 2025, the aforementioned Barbarians game and the first Test against Australia last summer.

But the autumn series will be seen as a major opportunity to get some wins on the board and climb back up the world rankings, where Wales were as high as sixth just three years ago.

And with the new-look WXV feeding into 2029 Rugby World Cup qualification - and a first ever Women's British and Irish Lions tour of New Zealand next September - there is plenty at stake for this group of pre-season players.

title: Al-Hilal open talks to sign Arsenal winger Martinelli
description: Saudi Arabian club Al-Hilal open negotiations with Arsenal over a move for Brazil forward Gabriel Martinelli.
fullText:
Arsenal have held talks with Saudi Arabian club Al-Hilal over the sale of winger Gabriel Martinelli.

The Brazil international is free to leave the club this summer, with manager Mikel Arteta making it clear to the attacker that he is not in his plans.

Turkish club Galatasaray showed interest in Martinelli earlier this summer but the Brazilian would not consider a move to Istanbul, despite Arsenal receiving a €45m (£38.54m) bid.

It is understood Al-Hilal have communicated to Arsenal that they are willing to bid higher than Galatasaray's offer.

Martinelli, who joined Arsenal from Brazilian side Ituano in 2019, has 12 months remaining on his deal at the Emirates Stadium.

Martinelli made 53 appearances in all competitions last season, scoring 11 goals, as the Gunners won the Premier League title.

But he was left out of the squad for their league opener against Coventry on Friday, which the Gunners won 3-0.

Former Arsenal striker Ian Wright was critical of Arteta's decision to omit Martinelli from the squad, as well as the club's treatment of the forward.

"The way Martinelli is being treated at the moment, it really makes me feel uncomfortable," Wright told Sky Sports.

"I know they might want him out, and a lot of people might say, 'yeah, it's time for him to move him on'. But there's ways of doing that and it should suit him as well, how he wants to leave."

BBC Sport understands that Arteta has made his position clear to Martinelli and explained his reasons why he has been left out of the squad.

Al-Hilal's interest in Martinelli runs alongside a move for Aston Villa striker Ollie Watkins.

The England international did not feature in Aston Villa's opening weekend defeat by Brighton on Sunday, with manager Unai Emery refusing to guarantee the forward would stay at Villa Park.

title: Jamieson takes Trump call after ending 14-year title wait
description: Scott Jamieson shoots a final round of 67 at the Nexo Championship to end his 14-year drought and earn a video call with President Donald Trump.
fullText:
Nexo Championship, Trump International Golf Links

-11 S Jamieson (Sco); -9 M Jordan (Eng); -7 A Sullivan (Eng); -6 Q Vidal (Spa), M Kinhult (Swe), K Nakajima (Japan)

Earning a first DP World Tour win in 14 years - and effectively saving his job by doing so - would be enough to disturb the composure of most golfers.

But as Scott Jamieson tried to come to terms with ending his drought at the Nexo Championship in Aberdeenshire, the 42-year-old Scot found himself speaking to President Donald Trump on a video call.

It has become tradition that the United States president contacts the winner at Trump International Golf Links in the immediate aftermath of their success.

And Glaswegian Jamieson was the bewildered recipient of the call this time, following compatriot Grant Forrest last year.

"He was very complimentary and it sounds like he was actually watching it," Jamieson told BBC Sport Scotland. "He said he was following along, so it was really cool... I mean he is the President of the United States."

That Jamieson kept his shape over a tense final few holes is testment to his resolve.

The Scot posted a final round 67 to come from three shots back and beat England's overnight leader Matthew Jordan by a couple of strokes.

He finished on 11 under par, having edged in front after then-leader South Africa's Shaun Norris was given a bizarre two-shot penalty for kicking away a loose divot on the fairway.

It was just Jamieson's second DP World Tour triumph, with his last success coming in 2012 at the Nelson Mandela Championship.

And given he looked at significant risk of losing his card, it has given Jamieson the security of knowing his playing rights are secure for next season at least.

"I didn't realise it had been 14 years," he conceded. "I practice every day and explore different ways to get better and sometimes it is like you are just banging your head against a wall. So the odd win here and there makes it all worthwhile.

"There have been times where I 've thought 'I might be losing my job here' so thankfully I don't need to worry about that for over the next few weeks.

"And hopefully this may open up some doors to kick on and try and push up the ladder."

Defending champion Forrest endured a tough Sunday, with a score of 80 taking him to a 10 over total.

But fellow Scots Euan Walker and Connor Syme were among those in a share of 10th place on four under.

title: GB's men defend team gold at European Championships
description: Great Britain produce a superb performance to successfully defend the men's team gold at the European Gymnastics Championships in Zagreb for the first time.
fullText:
Great Britain's men produced a superb performance to successfully defend their team gold at the European Gymnastics Championships in Zagreb for the first time.

Courtney Tulloch, Joe Fraser, Harry Hepworth, Jonas Rushworth and Sol Scott took gold with a score of 246.728 points after a tense battle with World Gymnastics Group 2 (WG2/Russia) went down to the final routine.

"This means everything, it's about consistency in team competitions, fighting through routines, pushing till the end and that's exactly what we did," said Fraser, who won gold in the high bar and bronze in the parallel bars on Saturday.

"I'm unbelievably proud of each and every member of this team."

Britain, gold medallists a year ago in Leipzig, finished third in the qualifiers after making several mistakes, but made a strong start to the final on the pommel, rings and vault, and held the lead at the halfway stage.

However, mistakes on the parallel bars and high bar meant there was less than a mark separating Britain and WG2 heading into the final rotation.

It all came down to Hepworth, who followed up his individual floor bronze medal performance on Friday with another big score on the floor to secure gold.

"It got close towards the end but we held our nerve and were absolutely delighted," said Fraser.

"The team competition is the big one and we've won it again, incredible."

Qualifying for the men's team final meant Britain had already secured a place at the World Gymnastics Championships in October in Rotterdam, which will serve as the first Olympic qualifying event for the 2028 Games in Los Angeles.

Earlier this week, Britain retained team gold at the junior European Championships.

title: Peace through strength, Taiwan president says on China battle anniversary
description: Peace can only be secured through strength and not even an inch of territory can be sacrificed, Taiwan President Lai Ching-te said
fullText:
KINMEN, Taiwan, Aug 23 (Reuters) - Peace can only be secured through strength and not even an inch of territory can be sacrificed, Taiwan President Lai Ching-te ‌said on Sunday, visiting a sensitive frontline island to mark a key battle with Chinese ‌forces almost seven decades ago.

Taiwan has controlled the Kinmen and Matsu islands, which lie just off the Chinese coast, since the Republic of ​China government fled to Taipei in 1949 after losing a civil war with Mao Zedong's communists. No peace treaty or armistice has ever been signed.

In heavy rain, Lai laid a wreath and bowed at a memorial park for the 68th anniversary of the 1958 clash with Chinese forces, known as the start of the second Taiwan ‌Strait crisis — the last time Taiwanese and ⁠Chinese forces battled on a large scale.

Addressing veterans later, Lai expressed gratitude to those who "stood united and fought a bloody battle to repel Communist totalitarian aggression".

"Our resolve to ⁠unite in defending national sovereignty and safeguarding peace across the Taiwan Strait must never waver," Lai said. "Peace has never simply fallen from the sky."

The 1958 battle proves "that peace is secured through strength," he said, adding it was necessary to ​maintain "the spirit ​of never yielding an inch" of Taiwan, Kinmen and ​another group of islands, while continuously boosting military ‌spending.

China's Taiwan Affairs Office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

China views democratically governed Taiwan as its own territory and has repeatedly denounced Lai as a "separatist". He rejects Beijing's sovereignty, saying only Taiwan's people can decide their future, but has also offered talks with China.

Kinmen at its closest is less than 2 km (1.2 miles) from Chinese-controlled territory. In the 1958 battle, Chinese forces began more than a month of ‌bombardment of Kinmen, along with Matsu, including naval and air ​battles, seeking to force them into submission.

Taiwan fought back with support ​from the United States, though the crisis ​ended in a stalemate. Taiwan observes August 23 every year as the date it ‌fended off the Chinese attack.

China's coast guard has ​since early 2024 conducted regular "law ​enforcement" patrols around Kinmen in Taiwan-controlled waters, to Taipei's anger.

Referring to those patrols and other Chinese tactics, Lai said that for 68 years China had not stopped its "ambitions for external expansion for even ​a single day", bringing "unease" across the ‌Indo-Pacific.

Taiwan's planned defence spending next year will exceed T$1 trillion ($30 billion) for the first time, the ​government announced on Thursday, and Lai said he hoped for strong support for the budget.

title: Ferrari delay in moving Leclerc costly - Hamilton
description: Lewis Hamilton says Ferrari's delay in moving team-mate Charles Leclerc out of his way could have cost him second place at the Dutch Grand Prix.
fullText:
Lewis Hamilton says Ferrari's delay in moving team-mate Charles Leclerc out of his way could have cost him second place at Sunday's Dutch Grand Prix.

Hamilton finished fourth in Zandvoort, with Mercedes taking second and third - championship leader Kimi Antonelli finishing as runner-up after his Mercedes team-mate George Russell was ordered to let him past.

Hamilton came up behind Leclerc mid-race when he was on fresher tyres and asked to be let through so he could optimise his race against the Mercedes drivers.

But after the team asked Leclerc to pit, the Monegasque resisted, was left out for a further lap, and then ordered to come in again.

Hamilton said over the radio at the time: "Great way of wasting time, guys. Great job."

Hamilton later caught Russell in the closing stages of the race but ran out of time to pass him, his attempts hindered by a late virtual safety car.

The two Ferrari drivers finished nose to tail in fourth and fifth places, right behind Russell.

McLaren's Lando Norris won the race.

Hamilton, who is 59 points behind championship leader Antonelli, said the race was "definitely frustrating".

Norris and McLaren 'don't have car' to fight for title

Norris beats Antonelli to claim final Dutch GP win

Russell impresses as Norris shines - driver ratings

"I'm here to win and i think this team can win," Hamilton said.

"We couldn't win this race but to win championships you have to pick up every point and the last few races have been difficult with penalties and stuff.

"And then today I lost several seconds behind Charles, which I think ultimately could have made the difference in the end.

"My goal is to try and lead this team to the championship. We've got some work to do, for sure."

He contrasted Ferrari's actions with those of Mercedes.

With Russell in second, and caught by his team-mate Antonelli and the two Ferraris behind, Mercedes ordered the Briton out of the way of his team-mate late in the race. That was to ensure Antonelli lost no time and consolidated second place.

Hamilton said: "What's clear is I'm looking at them and seeing Mercedes. They executed. They got the car, they are fighting for the championship and did it straight away.

"Here, sitting back, it's something that we need to discuss."

Ferrari team principal Frederic Vasseur said: "If I look at the race now, I can do it frankly, but my issue is that we didn't tell Lewis that we were expecting him to go to the end, and it was not a matter of pushing.

"We didn't want to tell [Hamilton] the strategy at this stage, because we didn't want to disclose it to the competitors, because we wanted to keep him on track until the end [of the race].

"He was able to keep Antonelli behind him, and I think it would have been the right call. Charles was supposed to pit. We extended one lap, and it was a kind of confusion, but I'm not worried about this - everybody will be back in the briefing, they will have a clear picture about the race."

Hamilton also urged Ferrari to upgrade their engine as soon as possible.

"The one thing I'm definitely really proud of the team for bringing an upgrade here this weekend.," he said.

"We are getting closer to them, but it's just half a season we've been down in power.

"We really need to pick up the power if we're going to be anywhere near trying to fight for them, closing the gap to them."

He said Ferrari were losing 0.4secs on the straights to Mercedes at Zandvoort.

title: Signs that Jaissle's Newcastle are not to be written off
description: Newcastle United were predicted to struggle from the off by some pundits, but head coach Matthias Jaissle will take encouragement from aspects of their display even after conceding a late equaliser against Liverpool
fullText:
The fourth official had just signalled that five minutes of stoppage time had been added on at St James' Park.

It was the cue for Newcastle United manager Matthias Jaissle to frantically raise his arms up and down on the touchline in an attempt to whip supporters up for one final push.

"Sing your hearts out for the lads," the crowd responded.

Newcastle United were 2-1 up against Liverpool, but no one inside the stadium needed reminding of the history of this fixture, which has become synonymous with late drama.

Who could forget when Stan Collymore struck late in a 4-3 thriller at Anfield in 1996 to leave Newcastle legend Kevin Keegan slumped over the advertising hoardings?

Those memories were still clear on an evening both clubs came together to celebrate such an iconic figure.

No wonder, then, the whistles from the home supporters were deafening as Liverpool launched one final attack, which culminated in substitute Victor Munoz being brought down by a tired Lewis Hall inside the box.

Jaissle ripped off his blazer in anguish, having felt it was a "soft" decision from referee Stuart Attwell.

Such a feeling clearly informed his post-match address to his players after Liverpool midfielder Dominik Szoboszlai stepped up to equalise from the spot and land a familar late blow in this 2-2 draw.

"I cannot repeat everything because I could get in trouble and may need to pay some fines," Jaissle said in his news conference following a long pause.

"But, overall, I told them that I'm really proud of what I saw over the 90 minutes. This is a really top starting point."

It was certainly an eventful start, just the sort of topsy turvy fixture Keegan was synonymous with during his time in charge of Newcastle.

How fitting then that the club legend's family and several of his former players, including Alan Shearer, Rob Lee and Tino Asprilla, were among those in the directors' box.

They watched on as supporters' group Wor Flags unfurled a huge display before the game, which encompassed every seat in the stadium, including a timely banner in the Gallowgate End.

"I want people to dream about their football club," it read. "They should. We should all be dreamers at heart.

"Some people are the opposite and say, 'We can't do that'. But when you ask them why, they can't give a reason. Well, I say, 'Why not?'"

Those words are still relevant.

In the last 12 months, Newcastle have lost key players in Alexander Isak, Anthony Gordon, Sandro Tonali and Bruno Guimaraes while head coach Eddie Howe has also departed.

Newcastle are targeting further reinforcements, but all of the club's signings this summer have been aged 24 and under and have never played in the Premier League before.

Noting Jaissle has also never managed in the English top flight, some pundits predicted that Newcastle would struggle from the off as a result.

Just as Jaissle recognised there were those who did not think "we can play a good role in the Premier League", so did injured captain Dan Burn, who believes Newcastle are at their best when "it's us against the world",

Newcastle tapped into that and, indeed, the noise surrounding Isak's return, which only energised the crowd further against Liverpool.

"If you have this synergy between the fans and then the players delivering on the pitch, something special can be created," Jaissle said.

There were early glimpses of just what Jaissle's side could be - the intensity, the balls in behind, the grit, spirit and work rate.

Few embodied those qualities quite like new arrival Amar Dedic, who only completed his £30m move from Benfica on Tuesday, but what was just as striking was the performances of one or two of last summer's signings following difficult first seasons on Tyneside.

It was Anthony Elanga who opened the scoring against Liverpool with a well-taken finish into the bottom corner while Yoane Wissa, who set up substitute Joe Willock's second, is clearly relishing added responsibility under Jaissle.

It said it all that Wissa, a forward, won more duels (11) than any other Newcastle player on Sunday.

"The manager expects me to be a leader and lead the group," the 29-year-old told Sky Sports.

"He wants me to be winning balls, making sure everyone is going forward, going for the kill, and sometimes just be calm."

Jaissle saluted Wissa's display, even if he could not help but add he also had the chance to "kill the game" to make it 3-1.

This was Newcastle's achilles heel last season.

No other side dropped more points (27) from winning positions in 2025-26 and predecessor Howe was the first to admit last May that "anything can happen" after he was asked if such a habit could seep into this campaign.

Yet the reaction of those Newcastle supporters who stayed behind to applaud afterwards was telling on Sunday.

"We were there for each other if something went wrong," Jaissle said of his players.

"We acted like a unit. In such a short amount of time, this is a top starting point and the frustration was there as well, but these are the challenges we have now.

"With the pre-season, with the transition phase, it's normal. Today someone threw stones in the way and we need to take that out to be successful again."

title: Union for Boston Symphony Orchestra musicians authorizes first strike in ensemble's 145-year history
description: The union for Boston Symphony Orchestra musicians authorized the first strike in the ensemble's 145-year history on Saturday.  The Boston Musicians' Association issued a statement ahead of the expirat...
fullText:
LENOX, Mass. (AP) — The union for Boston Symphony Orchestra musicians authorized the first strike in the ensemble's 145-year history on Saturday.

The Boston Musicians' Association issued a statement ahead of the expiration of the union's three-year contract at 11:59 p.m. Sunday.

The orchestra and management have had strained relations since BSO decided in March to force out music director Andris Nelsons next summer after 13 seasons.

"In spite of the turmoil of the last six months caused by BSO's leadership decision to terminate the orchestra's musical director, Andris Nelsons, they have failed to agree to a collective bargaining agreement that would begin to restore the trust that they have destroyed and offer a fair contract to the musicians who are at the heart and soul of the BSO," the union said in a statement.

The union said management has not agreed to musicians' proposal for a mediator.

"We respect the musicians' right to take this step as part of the negotiating process," BSO CEO Chad Smith said in a statement. "Our focus remains on the negotiations and the ongoing constructive conversations. We are committed to reaching an agreement with competitive pay and benefits that enhances collaboration with the players."

The orchestra's season is scheduled to open Sept. 17.

Wyndham Clark said he is "one of the best players in the world" after he survived a fightback from Rory McIlroy to win the BMW Championship in Missouri.

Clark held a five-shot lead going into the final day, but saw his advantage evaporate as McIlroy drew level with seven holes left to play.

But Northern Irishman McIlroy could not take several opportunities to move ahead, and successive Clark birdies enabled the American to post a fourth-round 71 and finish the week 17 under par.

After pushing Clark all the way, McIlroy ended the day one under par to finish 13 under, four shots behind the winner.

"It was weird - I wasn't nervous but I was kind of out of it, making double bogies, I can't believe I didn't make anything on the greens. But I kept trying to get myself going," Clark told CBS Sports.

"I really started to swing free down the end. I was proud I didn't let it get away and was mentally strong.

"I'm one of the best players in the world. Everyone gives me a hard time and roots for other people, but I've come into my own. It's my best season yet coming off my worst year."

After losing his first-day lead with a second-round 69, McIlroy said he needed a "heroic effort" to catch Clark on the final day.

The back-to-back Masters champion fought hard to gain two shots as Clark dropped three, but missed a put on the 14th with the scores tied - and from there Clark recovered.

"I can't be too disappointed, I'm not playing well enough to be too disappointed to no win," McIlroy told CBS Sports.

"I had my chances, but Wyndham stepped up. The way he played the last three holes, he showed a lot of character."

title: How Hull kept plan to stun Man Utd secret
description: Hull City boss Sergej Jakirovic kept his plan to topple Manchester United on their Premier League return under wraps for weeks, assistant head coach Dean Holden tells Match of the Day.
fullText:
Hull City boss Sergej Jakirovic kept his plan to topple Manchester United on their Premier League return under wraps for weeks, assistant head coach Dean Holden told Match of the Day.

The Tigers produced a sensational 2-0 opening-weekend win over Michael Carrick's side on Saturday while deploying a back five.

Hull were making their first Premier League appearance in nine years after coming up through the play-offs last year.

First-half goals from defenders Semi Ajayi and Nobel Mendy gave them their first league win over United since 1974.

Jakirovic altered his tactics for the game, having watched a couple of United's pre-season matches, including the 4-2 defeat by AC Milan, engineered by former boss Ruben Amorim, when he repeatedly switched play to his wing-backs, which United's defence failed to cover.

When quizzed on the tactic, Holden told Match of Day: "We certainly didn't copy Ruben Amorim.

"Serg had it in the back of his mind for three or four weeks that he was thinking of playing a back five. He didn't want to give anything away in pre-season, so we played a back four.

"The easiest thing to do in preparation was using some of the Milan clips and Leeds the week before played a back three too, so that helped us with players where the systems looked similar."

Hull's win over United, who finished third in the Premier League last season, is perhaps even more remarkable given the Tigers only had 28% of possession.

But seeing limited amounts of the ball is not a cause for concern for Hull says Holden.

"We are comfortable without the ball, so it is not like we are coming up here having dominated the Championship and now we have to change," said Holden.

"We are comfortable in that mid-block, that is one of our biggest strengths. Counter-attack as well.

"Sunderland set the trend with Leeds in terms of teams who have come up, and for us, it is about belief.

"We have a group of lads who have done the hard yards, there is no real superstars in there.

"The manager is the same, very humble. Feet will be firmly on the ground."

Jakirovic's Hull were favourites to finish bottom of the Premier League, having only squeezed into the play-offs on the final day of last season.

They then became the first team to finish sixth and win the play-offs in 16 years - beating Middlesbrough in the final.

Just 15 months ago the Tigers had been close to being relegated to League One, only staying in the Championship on goal difference in 2024-25.

Three of the team who started their 1-1 draw against Portsmouth on the final day that secured their Championship status were in the team which beat United.

Former Oldham Athletic, Bristol City and Charlton manager Holden joined the Tigers that summer.

"We are aiming to stay in the league. It is the hardest thing to do and then you build on top of that," Holden added.

"But a win at home in the first game is beyond anyone's dreams really. The performance is the biggest thing, the confidence, the belief, will stand us in good stead."

title: Trump waves green flag to start IndyCar race through Washington streets
description: The president took a ceremonial lap of the track before the race, which is the culmination of a summer of events to mark the country's 250th birthday.
fullText:
US President Donald Trump was among hundreds of people who gathered to see the IndyCar race through the streets of Washington DC on Sunday, marking the culmination of a series of summer events to celebrate the country's 250th birthday.

Driver Kyle Kirkwood won the race, earning his seventh career Indycar win.

Ahead of the race, the president and First Lady Melania Trump took a ceremonial lap of the 1.7-mile track in his presidential limousine, The Beast.

As they reached the finish line, Trump's new Air Force One completed a flyover above the capital.

The Freedom 250 Grand Prix is the first time professional road racing has been hosted in the capital.

With a maximum speed limit of 55mph (89kmh), Washington DC has the lowest speed limit in the United States.

But on Sunday, some of the world's fastest drivers zoomed past the capital's famous monuments and museums at speeds of up to 190mph (306kmh).

The 25 professional drivers competing in the event face 147 laps featuring seven crucial turns, making a total 250-mile course - a nod to the nation's anniversary.

The drivers sped past the Washington Monument and museums on the National Mall, before passing a finish line with the US Capitol building in frame.

Similar to Formula 1, the IndyCar series is a road race featuring open-wheel, single-seater cars.

But unlike F1, where teams design and build their own cars, the engines in IndyCars come exclusively from Chevrolet or Honda.

Organisers of the Freedom 250 Grand Prix say about 140,000 people are expected to attend, with many given free general admission tickets through a lottery.

However, premium packages sold for $5,000 for a pair of passes.

The event has been a huge logistical and security lift for the city, and has led to widespread road closures, manholes being bolted down, and road resurfacing.

The Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport, which primarily runs domestic flights, has been under a three-hour airspace closure to accommodate the US military flyover.

The National Gallery of Art conducted vibration tests to ensure its priceless collection could withstand the powerful rumble of the engines.

On race day, however, the roar of celebration appeared to largely drown out any irritation. Many of those lining the circuit were there after winning tickets through a public lottery. Some wore Uncle Sam hats, while one woman came dressed as the Statue of Liberty. Families had travelled from across the country for what they saw as a once-in-a-lifetime event.

American driver Josef Newgarden told the BBC that the significance of racing through the capital was not lost on him.

"It's super unique. You might never see this again, and as an American driver, it's very special celebrating the 250th anniversary of the country," he said. "It's a beautiful city, and it's very surreal."

In other events earlier this summer, Trump hosted an Ultimate Fighting Championship event on the White House lawn, as well as a fireworks show on 4 July.

title: Norris and McLaren 'don't have car' to fight for title despite Dutch GP win
description: Lando Norris says he and McLaren "don't have the car I need to fight for a championship", despite a second consecutive win of the season at the Dutch Grand Prix.
fullText:
Lando Norris says he and McLaren "don't have the car I need to fight for a championship", despite a second consecutive win to open the second half of the Formula 1 season.

The Briton's victory in the final Dutch Grand Prix at Zandvoort, following on from his first win of the season in Hungary last month, was of the highest calibre.

As such, it raises the prospect of the sort of championship fightback staged by Red Bull's Max Verstappen against Norris himself last year.

After this race last year, Norris' team-mate Oscar Piastri had a 34-point advantage over the Briton and 104 over Verstappen. Yet Verstappen, after one of the all-time great fightbacks, finished the season just two points behind Norris as he won the title in Abu Dhabi

Norris' masterful victory in Zandvoort has left him 83 points off the lead, held by Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli, who he and McLaren passed on track after losing the lead at the chaotic start of the day.

Antonelli's team-mate George Russell is tied on points with Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton, 59 behind the Italian.

Mercedes lack money to develop car like rivals - Wolff

But while McLaren have made a major step forward with upgrades to their car that led to convincing wins in both Hungary and now the Netherlands, Norris believes that the car still has too many flaws to mount the sort of consistent attack Verstappen produced last year.

"I'm confident because we clearly have a strong car," he said. "We have a strong car in certain areas. It's not like last year where we were pretty good everywhere.

"We're very, very strong in high speed, and that's the place we've improved the car the most, is high-speed performance. No one matches us in high speed, and that's a good thing.

"My pace advantage to Mercedes in Turn Seven, Eight was crazy, but their advantage that they have to us in slow speed is also crazy.

"And therefore, I don't have the confidence to say, 'Yeah, I can easily fight for a championship for the rest of the season.'

"I know I've just won two races in a row and had two poles in a row, but at the minute I don't have the car I need to fight for a championship. And I know that's quite a big comment."

Norris' belief is based on his understanding that McLaren's slow-speed performance will be a handicap at the next race in Monza, and two races after that in Azerbaijan.

Both tracks are dominated by long straights, which penalise the McLaren's high drag compared to Mercedes, and have very few high-speed corners where the car's strength can compensate for its weaknesses in slow turns.

McLaren team principal Andrea Stella said: “If we can confirm our improvements in Monza, then we can look with some optimism at the remainder of the season.”

Norris' victory in Zandvoort, built around an off-set strategy and devastating pace once the cars were on the hard tyres in the second stint, underlined the level at which he is now operating.

As impressive as Verstappen's revival was last year, Norris' own in the second half of the season was almost as good, as both made up ground on Piastri.

And Norris believes he has built on the progress he made in his driving after a difficult start to 2025 to perform on an even higher plane in 2026.

"I was driving at a high level the second half of last year," he said. "It's tough to say, but I do think it's a trickier car to drive this year in some ways. And I think you can see that because the gaps between team-mates are often bigger this year, I would say, than it was last year.

"I do believe I'm able to understand situations better, to understand the car in a better way. It's still just horrible to drive, but I'm doing a better job at just understanding this, relaying this to my team, figuring stuff out.

"So, it's not just I'm driving better on track. I'm certainly eliminating my weaknesses on track, and I don't have so many, but it's also how I work off the track. And for me, yesterday to today is a perfect example of the work we put in overnight transformed our race and gave me the opportunity to win."

Team principal Andrea Stella said he believed Norris was driving better than ever.

"Lando is driving and operating at a very high level," Stella said. "He's driving at the level of a world champion.

"What I like the most of his journey in Formula 1 is that he keeps improving.

"After the start of the 2025 season, something clicked, which is not only a single click, but it's a way of working with Lando, for Lando, and that we are adopting also on Oscar's side now in particular.

"This approach has led Lando to continuous improvements.

"It's almost like I see Lando stronger and stronger race by race. Because I think this weekend was nowhere near a weekend in which we could fight for the victory for granted, especially after having seen the performance in the sprint (in which Norris was passed by Ferrari's Charles Leclerc and finished third).

"But we invested in trying to understand where was the opportunity from a tyre exploitation point of view and car improvement.

"And then when you have conditions in which the car slides in the race, there's not much grip, then I think he is the master in these kind of conditions."

A couple of months ago, before the British Grand Prix, and before McLaren had won a race this season, Norris admitted in an interview with BBC Sport "a little bit" of frustration at not being able to defend the title he won last year.

So it's perhaps no surprise that now he appears to have at least an outside chance of making a fist of it, he is not making any presumptions.

"One race at a time," he said. "I know a lot of people say it now, but it's the truth of it. There's no point thinking that far ahead.

"Obviously, two great weekends, but there's still plenty of things we can do better, and we need to do better if we want to fight for a championship.

"It's still harder than I would like, and I don't want a bigger gap, so we have to keep working hard. There's still plenty of races, plenty of opportunity for everyone. So, keep my head down, keep working, and they'll keep coming."

McLaren's progress has come in the context of stagnation at Mercedes, whose lack of an upgrade to their car since Canada in May has led to them being caught by McLaren and Ferrari, a situation that has raised eyebrows among rival teams.

The next Mercedes upgrade is not due until the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia in four races' time.

For Antonelli - who also faces a grid penalty at his home race in Italy next time out because he needs to take a new engine that exceeds his allowance as a consequence of early-season reliability problems - it cannot come soon enough.

"Now as a team we need to find a little bit of time because McLaren have done a huge step," he said.

"So for sure, in this race, it's going to be more difficult, it's going to be challenging, but we're ready to do our best and to maximise every opportunity.

"And then hopefully it's going to be our turn to bring the package that's going to give us a little bit of the upper hand again."

title: Relief for Iraola but Liverpool have work to do after snatching draw at Newcastle
description: Dominik Szoboszlai's injury-time penalty rescues a point at the start of the Andoni Iraola era - but Liverpool need to improv after below-par performance.
fullText:
When Liverpool came to Newcastle last August, there was utter jubilation as Rio Ngumoha scored a remarkable 100th-minute winner.

They scored late again this time around, through Dominik Szoboszlai's 99th-minute penalty, but it felt more like a sense of relief than joy as they rescued a point.

Andoni Iraola said afterwards that his side did not deserve to lose and, to their credit, they never gave up as they earned a 2-2 draw.

A defeat would have been Liverpool's first on the opening weekend since 2012-13. A draw will do wonders for their spirit but it will certainly not mask their concerns.

"It's probably not the result you want when you come in before the game but we definitely deserve this point and even more," Iraola told BBC Radio 5 Live.

"The team has never given up and we've recovered one point and probably the taste is better because we score in the last minute."

Iraola will be content with the outcome, given his side trailed twice at a raucous St James' Park.

But on the flight back to Merseyside on Sunday evening, he would have had time to consider the performance, which highlighted why his squad needs more depth.

"You're expecting Liverpool to get top four this season at least but they didn't look like a top four team today," former Scotland winger Pat Nevin told 5 Live.

"There are more players to come in, so you can't make a real decision on how their season is going to go.

"There's a definite lack of creativity and somehow they must get the best out of Florian Wirtz and Alexander Isak because you certainly didn't get the best out of them today."

All eyes were on Wirtz and Isak - the Sweden striker, signed from Newcastle in a drawn-out saga last September, was booed relentlessly whenever he touched the ball. Wirtz did start positively, but was replaced just after the hour mark after Newcastle went 2-1 up.

Isak had 28 touches and looked fired up but wasted a brilliant opportunity in the second half - the kind of which he would take regularly when he was at Newcastle.

Both of them, signed for nine-figure fees last summer, will know that their overall output and connection must improve over the coming weeks and months.

This remains a Liverpool side offering more questions than answers.

One significant question is the Cody Gakpo conundrum, which will roll into the final week of the transfer window.

If Liverpool do bring in two more attacking players then Gakpo may leave.

The club have been linked with Paris St-Germain's Bradley Barcola and Ibrahim Mbaye and have had two bids rejected for Brighton's Yankuba Minteh.

Yet Dutchman Gakpo was Liverpool's best player at Newcastle and took his goal brilliantly - while there was another positive in the performance of Spanish forward Victor Munoz on his Liverpool debut from the bench.

Munoz won the late penalty after replacing Ngumoha but Iraola's decision to take off the English teenager off after just over an hour summed up how much he struggled down the right.

Ngumoha will turn 18 next week and has preferred to play down the left throughout his youth career but failed to have an impact on the other side.

With Iraola determined to have his wingers able to play on both sides, it remains to be seen if that experiment persists once Liverpool get more attackers in.

What is for certain is that Iraola needs more options. Once Munoz and Alexis Mac Allister came on in the 63rd minute, Iraola's remaining bench options were: Giorgi Mamardashvili, Ronald Araujo, Wataru Endo, Kostas Tsimikas, Trey Nyoni, James McConnell and Lewis Koumas.

Defensively, both Milos Kerkez and Jeremie Frimpong had poor games at full-back and Liverpool were undone on the counter attack for both of the goals they conceded.

The lack of a defensive midfielder showed and it was revealing to see Iraola use Mac Allister just ahead of the back four after Joe Willock put Newcastle 2-1 up.

Liverpool have now conceded more goals via fast breaks in all competitions than any other Premier League team since the start of last season - nine.

All that and more will be food for thought for the new Liverpool boss but this was a relatively positive start to life under Iraola - who prefers to wait until the day after the match for a debrief.

"I've liked a lot of the things I've seen from the team," he said. "There's definitely things to improve like the goals but I've seen a lot of things I've liked from the team. I've liked the energy, especially the players coming from the bench. I think we finished the game quite strong physically."

"We will never give up. I can guarantee you that," Szoboszlai told Sky Sports. "We have to fight every time - all day long during the 90 minutes. Everybody who came off the bench also made an impact as well. We need the whole squad and we need to be ready."

That desire was never a cause for concern on Tyneside. But this Liverpool squad must improve, both in terms of quality and quantity.

title: What will it take to stop the England hangovers?
description: Yet again, England are dealing with a player involved in a late-night incident. Only strong action will ensure there are no more, writes Stephan Shemilt.
fullText:
Yet again, the England men's cricket team is picking through the wreckage of a late-night misdemeanour.

The latest stain on the game's reputation is a result of pictures of fast bowler Brydon Carse in handcuffs and surrounded by police officers outside a nightspot in Derby. His Durham team-mate Matthew Potts is in the images, while former England captain Ben Stokes appears in the background.

If you're keeping score, we're now up to eight England players involved in incidents of this kind since Halloween last year.

Harry Brook was punched by a nightclub bouncer in Wellington, with Jacob Bethell and Josh Tongue present. Ben Duckett was filmed drunk in Noosa, then Stokes and Gus Atkinson were there when a member of England's security staff was struck in a London nightclub in June, breaching a curfew in the process.

To put it another way, there are 30 men currently on England central contracts. More than a quarter of them have been caught up in bother in the past 10 months. Of the four separate incidents, two have involved punches being thrown and another was a police matter.

In Carse's case, the time spent in handcuffs came days after new England Test captain Joe Root called on his players to be "really good role models, good human beings".

Root was speaking the day before England's first Test against Pakistan, for which Carse was part of the squad. The match was scheduled to still be ongoing when he found himself in the hands of the police.

It is understood that Carse was not arrested. Both the England and Wales Cricket Board (ECB) and the Cricket Regulator will work to establish what happened. There are early suggestions he was denied entry back into a nightclub, or he had a drink poured over him.

Carse was also not specifically on England duty at the time. He was released from the first-Test squad to play for Durham away at Derbyshire and was scheduled to report to Lord's for the second Test on Monday.

As of Sunday evening, he remains part of the squad for the second Test. England will take time to gather some information before a decision on his involvement is made.

Root warned his squad to "be adults" when he abolished the midnight curfew - in his first act as captain - that came into place after previous incidents. As part of that move, guidelines advising players about not drinking alcohol on the day before, during or after a game, or in public, have also been removed.

There is a duty of care towards Carse. Two years ago, the 31-year-old was banned for historical betting offences and rebuilt his career to become an England regular in all three formats. No bowler has more Test wickets for England than Carse's 58 since he made his debut in October 2024.

But there is also a deep sense of anger and frustration within the ECB at having to deal with another error of judgement by a high-profile player. Supporters will take their own view, among them a sense that the behaviour of these players is now beyond parody.

Does someone have to be left out of a squad or given a meaty suspension for the penny to drop? This might be the opportunity for Root to stamp his authority on a new era.

Naturally, there will once again be the debate about not denying players their freedom or stopping them from enjoying a victory.

For Carse, a Saturday night out came less than 48 hours before he is scheduled to report for England. He is only a tweaked hamstring away from playing in a Test at Lord's on Thursday.

Perhaps more damning is the kind of trouble this group of England players seem to find. Two punch-ups and a set of handcuffs. It also does not appear to have dawned on them that they are high-profile individuals, likely to attract attention, with footage finding its way to social media, as happened with Carse.

And what about Stokes, who, despite being retired, remains an employee of the ECB via his central contract.

As the former captain, should Stokes have been conscious about Carse being in that situation? What about the trouble in which Atkinson found himself alongside Stokes in June?

Three weeks ago, Stokes denied the England team has a drinking culture, but rather that the game itself has a problem. What has Stokes done to distance himself or those around him from that drinking culture?

Now there is a wait to see what happens next. The ECB only became aware of the incident on Sunday afternoon. The governing body will take a breath overnight and decide if Carse needs to be removed from the Test squad.

Perhaps, on Tuesday, director of cricket Rob Key will once again explain why the players he manages cannot keep themselves out of trouble. In the aftermath of the Stokes-Atkinson incident in June, Key denied that England have become a "national embarrassment". He may be asked again.

Key also might be asked about the whereabouts of new Test coach Stephen Fleming, who does not take up his post until the winter. Might Carse have been less inclined to step out of line had the new sheriff been in town?

Well, here is another situation for England to manage. Only strong action will ensure there are no more.
